title: Interference, phase and coherence
prior_knowledge_summary: When waves overlap, their signed displacements add by the principle of superposition.
Diffraction can spread waves so that they overlap after gaps or around obstacles.
Topic 7 established wavelength, phase and wave graphs.
new_learning: Interference from superposed waves; coherence; phase and path-difference conditions.
not_yet_taught: conditions for observing clear fringes in practical systems

learning_outcomes.statement: Understand the terms interference and coherence.

evidence_basis.note: P2 evidence supports coherence definitions, phase and path-difference reasoning, and resultant-amplitude explanations. No P1 lesson assignment inferred.

blocks.title: How can two waves make still water?
content: Two identical ripples reach one point at the same time. Sometimes the water moves more than either ripple would cause alone. At another point, the water can be momentarily still. How can adding two waves produce both outcomes?
The answer depends on the signed displacements that arrive and on whether their relative phase stays predictable.

figure.purpose: Create the interference puzzle through two contrasting outcomes.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper prediction sketch with two equal pulse pairs approaching two points. One pair has matching upward displacements and one has equal opposite displacements. Leave the result boxes blank.
figure.alt_text: Two pairs of equal wave displacements approach points where they may reinforce or cancel.

blocks.title: Superposition is the adding rule

controlled_definitions.displayed_content: when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements

content: When waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements. Add with signs. Two upward displacements reinforce; an upward and an equal downward displacement cancel.
Interference is the pattern of reinforcement and cancellation produced when waves overlap. Superposition is the rule used at each point. Interference is the resulting behaviour across points or time.

figure.purpose: Distinguish the displacement-adding rule from the interference outcome.
figure.brief: Colourful hand-drawn three-row displacement addition layout: +A plus +A gives +2A, +A plus -A gives zero, and unequal opposite arrows give the signed difference. Label superposition as rule and interference as outcome.
figure.alt_text: Signed displacement arrows show reinforcement, cancellation and partial cancellation.

blocks.title: Phase decides reinforce or cancel
content: If equal waves arrive in phase, crest meets crest and trough meets trough. Their displacements have the same sign, so the resultant amplitude is twice one amplitude. This is constructive interference.

If equal waves arrive in antiphase, a crest meets a trough. Their displacements have opposite signs, so they cancel completely. This is destructive interference. Unequal amplitudes at antiphase cancel only partly, leaving the difference in amplitude.

figure.purpose: Connect relative phase to constructive, complete destructive and partial destructive outcomes.
figure.brief: Three-panel teacher sketch of aligned wave traces: equal in-phase waves and doubled resultant, equal antiphase waves and zero line, unequal antiphase waves and smaller resultant. Use sparse phase labels.
figure.alt_text: Aligned wave traces compare constructive, complete destructive and partial destructive interference.

blocks.title: Path difference carries phase information
content: This is a formula to remember. Δx is the difference between the two distances travelled, λ is wavelength, and n is an integer: 0, 1, 2, and so on. Both Δx and λ use the same length unit.

A whole-number path difference, nλ, brings waves back into phase and gives constructive interference. An odd half-wavelength path difference, (n + 1/2)λ, brings them into antiphase and gives destructive interference for equal amplitudes.

figure.purpose: Make path difference visible as extra travelled distance.
figure.brief: Annotated route diagram from sources S1 and S2 to point P with one route unrolled beside the other. Mark an extra whole wavelength for constructive and an extra half wavelength for destructive in a comparison inset.
figure.alt_text: Two routes to a point show whole-wavelength and half-wavelength path differences.

blocks.title: A path-difference decision
content: Two in-phase water-wave sources produce wavelength 4.0 cm. A point is 22 cm from one source and 30 cm from the other. The path difference is |30 - 22| cm = 8.0 cm. Carry the unit: Δx = 8.0 cm.

Now compare with wavelength: 8.0 cm / 4.0 cm = 2.0, so Δx = 2λ. This is a whole-number multiple, so the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively. A direct route-length subtraction checks the result: the longer route contains exactly two extra cycles.

figure.purpose: Teach the complete route from distances to an interference conclusion.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn annotated worked layout with sources, point, routes 22 cm and 30 cm, then a three-box flow: subtract routes, divide by wavelength, classify whole or half wavelength. Do not resemble an official diagram.
figure.alt_text: A worked route diagram uses a path difference of 8.0 cm and wavelength 4.0 cm.

blocks.title: Coherence keeps the outcome stable

controlled_definitions.displayed_content: a constant phase difference between two waves

content: Coherence is a constant phase difference between two waves. The constant need not be zero. Coherent waves can keep a fixed non-zero phase difference, so the reinforcement and cancellation positions remain stable.

It is tempting to say coherent means in phase. That feels natural because in-phase waves are easy to picture, but it is too narrow. In phase is one possible constant phase difference. The scientific test is whether the phase difference stays constant.

Use this route: confirm overlap, find relative phase directly or from path difference, apply signed superposition, then state constructive, destructive or partial interference. Apparatus details and the practical conditions for clear fringes come next lesson.

figure.purpose: Correct the coherence misconception and consolidate the reasoning route.
figure.brief: Split teacher sketch: two wave traces with a fixed quarter-cycle offset across three times labelled coherent, and two traces with a drifting offset labelled not coherent. Add a compact overlap-phase-add-classify flow chart.
figure.alt_text: One wave pair keeps a constant phase offset while another pair drifts in relative phase.

concepts_taught: interference as reinforcement and cancellation from superposition
constructive and destructive interference from phase
misconceptions_addressed: Interference and superposition mean exactly the same thing.
Coherent waves must be in phase.
Antiphase waves always cancel completely even when their amplitudes differ.
skills_students_can_now_use: Distinguish interference from the principle of superposition.
Define coherence using constant phase difference.
Predict constructive or destructive interference from phase or path difference.
Account for incomplete cancellation when amplitudes differ.
next_lesson_can_assume: Whole-wavelength path differences give constructive interference for in-phase sources.
Odd-half-wavelength path differences give destructive interference for equal waves from in-phase sources.
